Glaciate (verb) means to cover land with glaciers or ice sheets, and/or to erode, carve, and reshape that land through the movement of glaciers. In practice, both things happen together, so the word captures the full picture of what ice does to a landscape — burying it and transforming it.
The Two Sides of the Word

Side 1 — Covering: When a massive body of ice spreads over a region and buries it, that land is being glaciated. Think of Antarctica right now. Ice sheets sit on top of the entire continent, in some places over 4 kilometers deep. The land underneath is completely buried. That is glaciation in its most visual sense.

Side 2 — Reshaping: This is where the word gets its real weight. Glaciers are not static. They move — slowly, but with enormous force — and as they do, they grind and scrape the rock beneath them, pluck chunks of stone and carry them along, and deposit boulders, gravel, and a fine rock powder (called glacial flour) wherever they melt or retreat. This whole process of ice acting on the land — carving it, sculpting it, leaving material behind — is also what it means to glaciate.

These two sides are really one unified idea. You cannot have a glacier sitting on land without it also doing this erosive work. So when scientists say a region was "glaciated," they mean both: it was buried under ice, and that ice left a permanently altered landscape behind.
What Glaciated Land Actually Looks Like

The effects of glaciation are visible all over the Earth today, even where there is no longer any ice. This is important to understand because the word "glaciate" is very often used in the past tense — describing something that happened long ago but whose results we can still see.

During the last Ice Age, which peaked roughly 20,000 years ago, enormous ice sheets glaciated vast portions of the Northern Hemisphere. Most of Canada, much of northern Europe, and large parts of northern Asia were buried under ice sometimes more than 3 kilometers thick. When that ice eventually retreated, it left behind entirely new landscapes.

The Great Lakes of North America were carved out by glaciers. The dramatic fjords of Norway — those long, steep, sea-flooded valleys — are glaciated valleys. The flat, rich plains of the American Midwest are blanketed in sediment that glaciers deposited as they retreated. The smooth, rounded hills of Scotland? Shaped by ice. Every one of these landscapes is the direct result of glaciation.
How the Word Is Used in Real Sentences

You will encounter "glaciate" most often in these forms:

Glaciated (past tense or adjective) — by far the most common form. It describes land that was once covered and sculpted by glaciers, even if the ice is long gone. For example: "The glaciated valleys of the Alps were formed over thousands of years." Or used as an adjective: "Glaciated terrain is often rocky, uneven, and dotted with lakes."

Glaciation (noun) — the process itself. For example: "Repeated glaciation over millions of years completely transformed the landscape of northern Europe."

Glaciating (present participle) — used when the process is actively happening right now. For example: "The advancing ice sheet is slowly glaciating the surrounding land."
A Key Nuance — Active vs. Former Glaciation

There is an important distinction worth knowing. Some land is currently being glaciated — meaning glaciers are on it right now, actively covering and reshaping it. Greenland and Antarctica are clear examples. Other land was glaciated in the past but is now ice-free — yet we still call it "glaciated" because the ice left its mark permanently. Much of northern Canada, Scandinavia, and the British Isles falls into this second category. Both uses of the word are correct and common; the context usually makes clear which one is meant.

To glaciate = to cover land with glaciers or ice sheets, and to carve and reshape that land through the movement and force of that ice.

If you ever see the word in a geology book, a geography article, or a nature documentary, it is always pointing to this: the powerful, slow, transformative relationship between moving ice and the land beneath it.
